title: Oak Trees Keep Pulling in Carbon Long After They Stop Growing
hook: Climate models often assume photosynthesis and tree growth rise and fall together. Oak trees just showed that a third or more of their yearly carbon capture happens after growth has already stopped.
key_points: Oak trees across the eastern U.S. and California kept photosynthesizing for months after their growth season ended.
Eastern oaks grew from May to July but kept photosynthesizing through October; about 36% of their annual carbon uptake happened after growth had stopped.
California oaks showed a similar pattern, with roughly 26% of yearly carbon uptake occurring post-growth.
The findings challenge a common climate-model assumption that more photosynthesis automatically means more long-term carbon storage as wood.
Since much of that late-season carbon becomes leaves or short-term fuel rather than durable wood, forests may store less carbon long-term than current models predict.
content_html: It seems intuitive: if a tree is photosynthesizing more, it must be storing more carbon as wood. A new multi-site study of oak trees says that link is weaker than climate models assume.
extra_html: Combining satellite measurements of photosynthesis, hourly carbon dioxide readings above the tree canopy, trunk sensors tracking size changes, and decades of tree-ring and temperature records, researchers found that eastern U.S. oaks grew from May to July but kept photosynthesizing all the way through October — with about 36% of their entire year's carbon uptake happening after growth had already stopped. California oaks showed a similar pattern, capturing roughly 26% of their annual carbon post-growth. The catch is where that late-season carbon goes: mostly into leaves and short-term metabolic fuel, not durable wood, which is where forests store carbon for the long haul. As the lead researcher put it, most models assume that photosynthesis means growth — but this data shows that link doesn't hold, suggesting forests may lock away less carbon over time than current climate models predict, especially as warming and weather variability increase.

related.title: Photosynthesis
related.hook: Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, and using only sunlight, build sugar — releasing the oxygen you're breathing right now.

related.title: Why Plants Run the Planet
related.hook: Nearly every breath you take and every meal you eat traces back to plants — they make the oxygen, anchor the food chain, and lock away carbon for the whole biosphere.

flashcards.prompt: What surprising pattern did researchers find in when oak trees absorb carbon?
flashcards.back_html: Oak trees keep photosynthesizing and absorbing carbon for months after their growth season ends — up to about 36% of their annual carbon uptake happens after growth has already stopped.

flashcards.prompt: What common climate-model assumption does this finding challenge?

choices.text: That more photosynthesis automatically means more long-term carbon storage as wood
That trees photosynthesize at all outside of summer
That oak trees are a major source of atmospheric carbon

flashcards.explanation_html: Many climate models assume photosynthesis and growth (and thus long-term wood carbon storage) rise and fall together — this study shows that link doesn't hold for oaks.

flashcards.prompt: Why does late-season carbon uptake matter less for long-term storage than growth-season uptake?

choices.text: Much of it becomes leaves or short-term metabolic fuel rather than durable wood
The tree releases it back into the atmosphere the same day
It gets absorbed by soil microbes instead of the tree

flashcards.explanation_html: Carbon captured after growth has stopped tends to go toward leaves and short-term metabolic needs rather than wood, which is where carbon gets stored for the long term — so forests may sequester less durable carbon than expected.
